hints: Start by using the dashed line in Fig. 8.1 as a map - everything above it is in one kidney region and everything below it, looping down toward the pelvis, is in the other.
Follow the tubule in order from Bowman's capsule - the first coiled part is proximal, then comes the long hairpin loop down into the medulla, then the second coiled part back up near the top.
Label A is the second coiled region after the loop, B is the whole upper region containing the capsule and both coiled tubules, and C is the long U-shaped loop itself.
walkthrough:
Picture Where You Are In The Kidney**
Think of the kidney as having an outer layer called the cortex where filtration and much selective reabsorption happen, and an inner layer called the medulla where concentration gradients are built. In Fig. 8.1 the dashed line separates them, so the bracket B covering Bowman's capsule and the twisted tubules is the cortex.

Trace The Nephron In Order**
Fluid filters into Bowman's capsule, then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, then down and up in the long hairpin called the loop of Henle which dips deep into the medulla, then into the distal convoluted tubule before entering the collecting duct. That makes C the loop of Henle.

Pin Down A**
Label A points to the coiled tubule after the loop has returned to the cortex, sitting close to the collecting duct. That second coil is the distal convoluted tubule, where fine tuning of ions and pH occurs.
Final answer: A - distal convoluted tubule; B - cortex; C - loop of Henle.

hints: Look at the key first and match each line style to its y-axis - solid line to left axis for concentration and dashed line to right axis for flow rate, then read left to right as ADH increases.
For each curve separately, decide if it slopes up or down as blood ADH goes from 10 to 90 arbitrary units, and think about what that means for water reabsorption.
Pick two clear paired values with full units to prove the trend, for example at low versus high ADH, and also state how the two urine variables relate to each other.
walkthrough:
Read The Solid Line - Urine Concentration**
The solid line uses the left axis in $mmol \ dm^{-3}$. As blood ADH rises from 10 to about 60 arbitrary units, concentration rises steeply from about $200$ to $1100 \ mmol \ dm^{-3}$, then levels off toward about $1190 \ mmol \ dm^{-3}$ at 90 units. More ADH means more concentrated urine.

Read The Dashed Line - Urine Flow Rate**
The dashed line uses the right axis in $cm^{3} \ min^{-1}$. As ADH rises over the same range, flow rate falls steeply from $15$ to about $3 \ cm^{3} \ min^{-1}$, then falls more slowly to about $1.5 \ cm^{3} \ min^{-1}$. More ADH means less urine produced per minute.

Link The Two Trends**
The two variables move in opposite directions. When flow rate is high, little water has been reabsorbed so urine is dilute. When ADH is high, much water is reabsorbed so only a small volume of highly concentrated urine remains. Always quote data with units to earn full credit.

Final answer: As blood ADH concentration increases, urine concentration increases and urine flow rate decreases, so as flow rate decreases concentration increases. e.g. at ADH 10 arbitrary units urine concentration is $200 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ and flow rate is $15 \text{ cm}^{3} \text{ min}^{-1}$, whereas at ADH 90 arbitrary units concentration is $1190 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ and flow rate is $1.5 \text{ cm}^{3} \text{ min}^{-1}$.

hints: Start with the trigger - low blood water potential means more ADH is released, so think about where that ADH arrives and what type of molecule it is for binding.
Remember ADH cannot enter the cell, so it must trigger a relay inside - think about the classic membrane receptor to enzyme to small internal messenger pathway.
The end effect is about water channels stored inside the cell - think about how vesicles can quickly change the cell surface membrane.
Connect the change in membrane proteins to a change in permeability and then to net movement of water by osmosis.
Finish the story by explaining where the water goes and how this corrects blood water potential and produces the concentrated, low-volume urine seen in Fig. 8.2.
walkthrough:
ADH Binding Starts The Signal**
When blood water potential falls, more ADH reaches the kidney in the blood. ADH is a peptide hormone so it binds to specific receptors on the outer surface of the collecting duct cell membrane. This is cell signalling, not ADH entering the cell.

A Second Messenger Amplifies Inside**
The occupied receptor activates a G protein which activates the enzyme adenylate cyclase. That enzyme makes cyclic AMP, called cAMP, which acts as a second messenger inside the cytoplasm. cAMP then activates protein kinase enzymes.

Aquaporins Are Inserted By Exocytosis**
Inside the cell there are vesicles in the cytoplasm whose membranes contain aquaporin water channel proteins. Activated protein kinase causes these vesicles to move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane. Fusion inserts many extra aquaporins into the membrane facing the lumen and the membrane facing the tissue fluid.

Permeability To Water Rises**
Aquaporins are specific channel proteins for facilitated diffusion of water. With more of them, the collecting duct cells and the whole duct wall become much more permeable to water. Because the medulla tissue fluid around the duct has a low water potential from the loop of Henle gradient, water leaves the dilute tubular fluid by osmosis.

Blood Is Conserved And Urine Concentrates**
That water passes through the cells into the medulla and then into the blood capillaries, raising blood water potential back toward normal. Less water is left in the tubule, so a small volume of highly concentrated urine flows to the pelvis. This is exactly why high ADH in Fig. 8.2 gives low flow rate and high concentration.

Final answer: ADH binds to receptors in the cell surface membrane of collecting duct cells, activating G protein and adenylate cyclase to produce cAMP second messenger which activates protein kinase. This causes vesicles containing aquaporins to fuse with the cell surface membrane, inserting more aquaporins so the membrane becomes more permeable to water. More water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the tubule lumen into the blood, concentrating the urine.
